57.title: The well
57.hook: they drop him into a well, and Allah inspires him that one day he'll tell them what they did
57.carry: even in the well, a promise
57.tomorrow: The shirt and the false blood
57.howItsDone: Muslims often recite and reflect on Surah Yusuf in times of grief or hardship; the promise to Yusuf in the well is remembered as a sign that Allah reaches people where no one else can.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hasad, the brothers' plan, jealousy with repentance already scheduled. Your line was jealousy makes plans.

The brothers have their plan. Now they need their father to let the boy go. So they come to Ya'qub, all warmth. Father, why don't you trust us with Yusuf? We only wish him well. Send him with us tomorrow; he'll run and play, and we'll look after him. And Ya'qub says something that should chill them: it grieves me that you'd take him away, and I'm afraid a wolf might eat him while you're not paying attention. A wolf. He's handed them the words. They answer: if a wolf eats him, with all of us there, we'd be losers indeed. In the morning, the boy goes out with them.
screen: `FATHER, TRUST US WITH HIM.` → `I FEAR A WOLF.` → `HE GOES WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf, verse fifteen, tells the worst moment in almost no words. So when they took him away, and agreed to put him in the depths of the well. That's it. No struggle, no shouting, no boy's face. The Qur'an doesn't linger on the cruelty; it moves straight to what matters more. And We inspired him: you will surely tell them about this deed of theirs, while they do not realize. A boy, maybe still a child, at the bottom of a dark, damp well, his brothers' voices fading overhead. Into that darkness comes a message: this isn't the end. One day you'll stand in front of them and tell them what they did. It doesn't take him out of the well, or stop the caravan, or the slavery, or the prison that's coming. It gives him a thread to hold in the dark. And notice who it's for. Not the brothers; they don't hear it. Not Ya'qub; he's at home, waiting. Just Yusuf, alone, where nobody else can reach. The Arabic for the depths of the well is ghayabat al-jubb. Readers of the Arabic hear in ghayaba the root for what's hidden, unseen, the root of al-ghayb, the unseen world the Qur'an speaks of. The bottom of the well is where you vanish from sight, and that's exactly where the promise reaches him. Some years later, and a few days from now for us, we'll see it kept.

segments.voice: If you can, close your eyes or dim the light, and touch the edge of the darkest place you've been, or are in now; you don't need to relive it. Then imagine that, even there, something reached you, a voice, a memory, a promise, a person, and if nothing did, imagine what you'd want to hear now. If you pray, you can remember that Allah reached Yusuf at the bottom of the well.
The well. Where Yusuf's brothers left him, and where a promise found him: one day you'll tell them what they did. Today's word.

58.title: The shirt and the false blood
58.hook: they bring his shirt with false blood, and Ya'qub says: beautiful patience
58.howItsDone: Muslims often say "sabrun jamil" to themselves or to one another in times of loss, recalling Ya'qub's words, and sabr is counted among the central virtues of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the well, and a promise that reached a boy in the dark. Your line was even in the well, a promise.

It's evening. The brothers come home, and they're weeping. Loudly. Father, we went off racing each other, and we left Yusuf by our things, and a wolf ate him. Then, before he's said a word, they add: but you won't believe us, even though we're telling the truth. When someone tells you they're telling the truth before you've asked, you already know. And they have evidence: his shirt, stained with blood. Not his blood. The Qur'an calls it false blood. It is the news no father wants to hear. Today's word is what Ya'qub says next.
screen: `EVENING. THE BROTHERS WEEP.` → `A WOLF ATE HIM.` → `A SHIRT, WITH FALSE BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Ya'qub looks at the shirt. Commentators have long pointed out a detail: a wolf that eats a boy but leaves his shirt without a tear? He says: no. Your own selves have talked you into something. Then two words, in Arabic, sabrun jamil. Pickthall's old translation renders it "comely patience." Beautiful patience. Sabr: patience, endurance, holding steady. Jamil: beautiful. It isn't gritted-teeth patience, the kind that sighs loudly and tells everyone how much it's suffering. Muslim scholars have explained sabr jamil as patience without complaint to people. You can still grieve; you just don't turn the grief into a weapon against those around you. And he adds: Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe. He knows they're lying. He doesn't scream, or beat it out of them, or pretend to believe them. He names it, and then he waits. The mistake to avoid: sabr jamil doesn't mean feeling nothing. Later in this very surah, Ya'qub weeps for Yusuf until his eyes turn white with grief. When his sons tell him he'll grieve himself to death, he says: I only complain of my sorrow and grief to Allah. The tears are real. The complaint goes up, not out. Beautiful patience is a way of carrying pain, not a way of not having it. Ya'qub will carry this a long time. He says those two words again, later, when a second son is lost.

segments.voice: Find something that's hurting right now, a slight, an unfairness, a loss, and notice the part of you that wants to vent, to get the story out and get it agreed with; let the feeling be there, but for these two minutes, don't hand it to anyone. If you pray, you can do what Ya'qub did and tell it to Allah instead; if you don't, just hold it gently, like something fragile. And if something is truly harming you, telling someone who can help isn't complaining; that's wisdom.
Sabr jamil. Beautiful patience: grief that's real, carried without turning it on the people around you. Today's word.
Your line: beautiful patience. Two words, said over a shirt with false blood. Day fifty-eight, done.

59.title: Sold for a few coins
59.hook: a caravan pulls him out and sells him cheaply in Egypt
59.carry: the price they paid isn't your worth
59.howItsDone: Muslim teachers draw from Yusuf's sale the lesson that human judgments of worth are not Allah's, and point to 12:21, which says Allah is in full command of His affairs, though most people don't know it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sabr jamil, and a father who named the lie and then waited. Your line was beautiful patience.

A caravan of travelers comes by the well. They send their water-drawer, and he lets down his bucket. It comes up heavy. He looks in and shouts: good news! Here's a boy! For a boy who's been waiting in the dark, that sounds like rescue. Except the men up top aren't rescuers. They're traders. And a boy, to a trader, is something else.
screen: `A CARAVAN COMES BY.` → `THE BUCKET COMES UP HEAVY.` → `GOOD NEWS! A BOY!`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. They hid him away as merchandise, and sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams, counted out. The Arabic for that price is bakhs, a cheated, short-changed price, less than a thing is worth. And the verse adds: they thought little of him. The boy who dreamed the stars bowing, sold for pocket change by men who didn't much care. Commentators have noted that a price you can count, a few coins rather than a weighed amount, was itself a sign of how cheap it was. Now watch the next verse, because the Qur'an turns the whole scene around. The man in Egypt who bought him says to his wife: make his stay honorable. Perhaps he'll be of use to us, or we might take him as a son. Sound familiar? It should. Two weeks ago, in Pharaoh's palace, Pharaoh's wife, the woman tradition calls Asiya, looked at baby Musa and said almost the same words. Two boys, in two stories, taken into an Egyptian house by someone who saw what the world had missed. Then the verse says: and so We established Yusuf in the land, and Allah is in full command of His affairs, but most people don't know. The traders set the price. They didn't set his worth. The boy they sold for a handful of coins is, in the story's own words, being established. Nobody watching that sale could have guessed it.

segments.voice: Think of a time someone set a low price on you: passed over for the job, talked over in the meeting, treated like you were extra in your own family. Then gently separate two things, what they paid or thought or offered, and what you actually are, and say it to yourself slowly: that was their price, not my worth. If you pray, you can remember how the verse ends: Allah is in full command of His affairs.
Bakhs, a cheated price: what the traders paid for Yusuf, thinking little of him, while Allah was establishing him in the land.

60.title: The house of the Aziz
60.hook: the lady of the house tries to seduce him, and he says: I seek refuge in Allah
60.howItsDone: Muslims say a'udhu billah, "I seek refuge in Allah," before reciting the Qur'an, when angry, and when tempted; Yusuf's words in the house of the Aziz are a well-known example.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bakhs, sold for a few coins, a boy the traders thought little of. Your line was the price they paid isn't your worth.
screen: `THE PRICE THEY PAID ISN'T YOUR WORTH.`

segments.voice: Temptation rarely arrives when you're weak and alone in a dark alley. More often it shows up when life is going well. The job, the trust, the key to the building. Nobody's watching. Yusuf has grown up in the house of the man who bought him. The Qur'an calls that man al-Aziz, a title, something like the mighty one, a high official of Egypt. Yusuf has reached his full strength, and the verse says he's been given wisdom and knowledge. He's trusted, he's handsome, he lives under their roof. And the lady of the house has noticed.
screen: `TEMPTATION WHEN THINGS GO WELL.` → `AL-AZIZ, A HIGH OFFICIAL.` → `THE LADY OF THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf, verse twenty-three, told with great restraint. She, in whose house he was, tried to turn him from himself. She closed the doors, and said: come. Yusuf's answer, in Pickthall's old translation: "I seek refuge in Allah!" In Arabic, ma'adha-llah. Then his reasons: he's my master, he's treated me well; and wrongdoers don't prosper. Who is my master? Commentators split. Some say the Aziz, who gave him a good home. Others say his Lord, Allah. The Arabic word, rabb, can carry both, and the verse may be holding both at once: loyalty to the man who trusted him, and to the God who made him. Then a verse commentators read in more than one way: she desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the clear sign of his Lord. What was the sign? The Qur'an doesn't say; commentators have offered many answers. What it does say is that Yusuf was human, the pull was real, and he turned. His phrase has a close cousin in daily Muslim life: a'udhu billah. The Qur'an tells its readers to seek refuge in Allah before reciting, and Muslims also say it when anger rises, or a bad thought knocks. Seeking refuge is not proving you're strong. It's admitting you need a place to run to, and running there. Yusuf didn't argue with the temptation, or out-think it. He named where he was going, and he went.

segments.voice: Think of the thing that tempts you most often, maybe small: the extra drink, the cruel comment, the scroll at two in the morning, the lie that would make things easier, and picture it knocking. Instead of arguing with it, picture turning and walking somewhere safe; if you pray, you can say a'udhu billah, I seek refuge in Allah, and let the words be the door you step through. If not, choose one word that means safe to you, and practice going there.
Ma'adha-llah, I seek refuge in Allah: what Yusuf said when the lady of the house closed the doors behind him.
Your line: I seek refuge. Short words, for the moment the doors close. That's sixty days.

61.title: Torn from behind
61.hook: the shirt is torn from the back, and a witness says that proves who ran
61.howItsDone: Muslims often point to the torn shirt as an example of Allah bringing the truth to light, and to Yusuf's calm answer as the way to respond when falsely accused.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ma'adha-llah, the house of the Aziz, and a young man who ran to refuge. Your line was I seek refuge.

He runs for the door. Yusuf has said I seek refuge in Allah, and now he does the most practical thing a person can do with temptation. She runs after him. They both race for it, the Qur'an says, and she catches hold of his shirt from behind, and it tears. Then the door opens, and there, standing in the doorway, is her husband. Everyone freezes. It's a moment straight out of a courtroom drama, except there's no courtroom and no lawyer. Just two stories, one husband, and a torn shirt.
screen: `HE RUNS FOR THE DOOR.` → `SHE CATCHES HIS SHIRT.` → `THE HUSBAND IN THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. She speaks first, fast: what's the penalty for someone who meant harm to your wife, except prison or a painful punishment? She doesn't even say what he did; she jumps to the sentence. Yusuf answers simply: she tried to turn me from myself. That's all. Then a witness from her own family speaks. The Qur'an says only a witness of her household; who it was, the text doesn't say. Some commentators report it was a wise man of her family; others tell a story that it was an infant who spoke. The witness says: look at the shirt. If it's torn from the front, she's telling the truth and he's lying. If it's torn from the back, she's lying and he's telling the truth. It's almost a detective's rule. Someone lunging at you tears the front. Someone running from you gets caught from behind. The husband looks. Torn from behind. He says: this is your scheming. To Yusuf: leave this alone. And to his wife: ask forgiveness for your wrong. Notice what Yusuf did not do. No speech. No attack on her. He said one true sentence and let the evidence speak. And this is the second shirt in the surah. The first came home with false blood on it, and it lied. This one is torn from behind, and it tells the truth. There's one more shirt still to come in this story. Keep an eye on the shirts.

62.title: The knives and the fruit
62.hook: the city's women, cutting fruit, see Yusuf and cut their hands
62.howItsDone: Muslims describe Yusuf as having been given great beauty, citing the hadith of the night journey, and read the banquet scene as a reminder that beauty, like wealth or power, is a trust and a test.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qamis, torn from behind, a shirt that told the truth. Your line was the shirt tells.

Some things you can't keep inside a house. The Aziz told Yusuf to let the matter drop, but soon the city is talking. The Qur'an lets us hear the gossip. Women of the city are saying: the Aziz's wife is chasing her young servant. He's struck her heart with love. We think she's clearly lost her way. Gossip over dinner sounds much the same in any century. And she hears about it. She doesn't argue with the gossip. She invites the gossips to dinner.
screen: `THE CITY IS TALKING.` → `STRUCK HER HEART WITH LOVE.` → `AN INVITATION TO DINNER.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. She sends for them, prepares a banquet with cushions to recline on, and hands each of them a knife. Then she tells Yusuf: come out to them. When they see him, they're so struck that they cut their own hands. They say: Allah preserve us! This is no human being. This is nothing but a noble angel. And she says: there. That's the one you blamed me for. Now, the fruit. The title says fruit, and that's how the story is usually pictured, women peeling something when he walks in. But the Qur'an doesn't mention fruit at all, only a banquet and knives. The fruit comes from the commentators, who wondered what the knives were for. Some said citrons; some said other things. The text is silent, and the image stuck anyway. The gossips' word for her love is worth a look too: shaghafaha hubban. Commentators explain shaghaf as the thin covering around the heart. Love had gone right through it. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, describing his night journey in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, said he met Yusuf, who had been given half of beauty. So this story takes beauty seriously. It isn't sinful to be beautiful, and Yusuf did nothing here but walk into a room. But beauty tested everyone in it. The women who mocked, then couldn't hold a knife steady. The wife, who stopped hiding what she felt. And Yusuf, who is about to discover that being admired can be its own kind of trap.

segments.voice: Think of the last time something striking caught your eye, a face, a sunset, a perfect car, and let your reaction come back: attraction, envy, the urge to take a photo, to own it, to compare yourself. Look at it with curiosity, not shame, and then at how you feel about your own looks, anxious, proud, invisible. If you pray, you can ask for eyes that see beauty without being ruled by it.
Shaghaf, the covering around the heart: what love went through, the gossips said, when they saw Yusuf and cut their own hands.

63.title: Prison, chosen
63.hook: Yusuf prays that prison is dearer to him than what they ask of him
63.howItsDone: Muslims honor Yusuf's choice of prison as a model of chastity and integrity, often alongside the hadith of the seven whom Allah shades, which includes one who refuses a woman of rank and beauty, saying "I fear Allah."

segments.voice: Yesterday: shaghaf, a banquet where beauty tested everyone. Your line was beauty is a test too. Today, the end of the week.

Keep quiet and keep the job, or speak up and lose it. Go along with the group, or walk home alone. The comfortable wrong thing, or the uncomfortable right one. Usually the price of the right one is a bad week, an awkward dinner. Yusuf's price is a cell. After the banquet, the pressure isn't coming from one woman anymore. The wife has said it in front of everyone: if he doesn't do what I tell him, he'll be imprisoned, and humiliated. And the Qur'an suggests the others are pressing him too. He's cornered, in a comfortable house. And he turns and prays.
screen: `THE COMFORTABLE WRONG THING.` → `DO IT, OR PRISON.` → `CORNERED IN A GOOD HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf, verse thirty-three. He says: my Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they're calling me to. And unless You turn their scheming away from me, I'll lean toward them, and be one of the ignorant. Two things in that prayer. First, the choice. He isn't sentenced yet. He's asking for the cell over the comfortable house. Prison, the Arabic sijn, is dearer to him, more beloved, than an easy life with a compromise at the center. He'd rather lose his freedom than lose himself. Second, look how honest he is. He doesn't say, don't worry, I'm strong. He says: unless You help me, I'll slip. Remember his cry in the house of the Aziz, I seek refuge in Allah. Same man, same humility. And the next verse: so his Lord answered him, and turned their scheming away. Even after they'd seen the signs of his innocence, it seemed best to them to imprison him for a time. The innocent man goes to prison, and the story doesn't pretend that's fair. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in a hadith in Bukhari, named among the seven people Allah shades on the Day when there's no shade but His: a man called by a woman of rank and beauty, who says, I fear Allah. And that's the week. A boy in a well. A father's beautiful patience. Sold for coins. A house with closed doors. A torn shirt. A banquet. And now a cell, chosen.
screen: `PRISON IS DEARER TO ME.` · `UNLESS YOU TURN IT FROM ME.` · `HIS LORD ANSWERED HIM.` · `IMPRISONED ANYWAY, FOR A TIME.` · then, large: `THE PRISON WAS FREER.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where the easy option and the right one have split apart, maybe something small: telling the cashier they undercharged you, admitting a mistake before anyone finds it, skipping the gossip. Picture both roads, feel the comfort of the easy one, then picture choosing the other: what's the prison you fear, and is it really so bad? If you pray, you can borrow Yusuf's honesty: unless You help me, I'll slip.
Prison. The cell Yusuf chose over a comfortable compromise, and asked for help to keep choosing. Today's word.
Your line: the prison was freer. A locked cell, and a whole self inside it. See you tomorrow.
